title: Four requests and a group chat
note: Fictional unit, patients, and requesters. Your facility’s privacy policy, the data protection officer, and counsel come first.
intro: You are the medical records officer. On Friday at 09:15, the human resources office of a patient’s employer emails: they need Mr. Arturo Lim’s “complete medical records, including hepatitis status” to approve his work schedule around dialysis. The email is from the company’s official address. There is no authorization from Mr. Lim on file.

choices.text: Reply that records are released only with the patient’s written authorization, and that for a schedule an employer usually needs only his dialysis schedule and a functional statement; tell Mr. Lim, and log the request and that nothing was released.
choices.feedback: Identity may pass, but authority fails: an employer needs the patient’s authorization. Scope fails too: the schedule, not the hepatitis status. The log shows the request and that nothing went out.

choices.text: Send the full chart; it is an official company address and they are helping him.
choices.feedback: A real company with a good purpose still fails authority and scope. Sending hepatitis results to an employer without the patient’s consent is a serious privacy breach.
choices.then: You stop before sending and reply asking for Mr. Lim’s authorization, offering a schedule statement.

choices.text: Ignore the email; employers never get records.
choices.feedback: With the patient’s authorization, an employer can receive schedule and functional statements. Silence leaves Mr. Lim without the help he needs. Explain the path and log the request.
choices.then: You reply with the authorization requirement and tell Mr. Lim.

n2.scene: At 11:00 a uniformed police officer comes to the counter and asks to see the dialysis records of a patient involved in a road accident last night, “for the report.”

choices.text: Explain politely that you cannot release or discuss records, take his name, unit, and contact details, log the request, and route it to the data protection officer or counsel.
choices.feedback: Police requests are not yours to decide. You log and route them; the data protection officer or counsel decides what, if anything, is released and on what legal basis.

vitals.log: Police request logged; routed to DPO

choices.text: Show him the chart; he is the police.
choices.feedback: A uniform is not legal authority to see a record. Requests from the police go to the data protection officer or counsel.
choices.then: You close the chart, log the request, and route it.

vitals.log: Police request logged; routed to DPO

choices.text: Ask him for a request letter, then decide yourself whether to release.
choices.feedback: A written request helps, but the decision is the data protection officer’s or counsel’s, not yours.
choices.then: You take the letter and route it.

vitals.log: Police request logged; routed to DPO

n3.scene: Mrs. Gloria Santos, reading a copy of her chart, says her hepatitis B status is recorded as “reactive.” She says her test was nonreactive and her vaccination card proves it. She wants it removed today.

choices.text: Log the request, verify her identity, route it to the author through the clinical correction workflow, keep the request with the record, and tell her the outcome in writing.
choices.feedback: Correction is her right, and patients reading their charts catch real errors. But a clinical entry is corrected by its author, with the disputed entry and her request kept on record.

vitals.log: Correction request logged; routed to author

choices.text: Delete the entry; she has proof.
choices.feedback: Never delete or overwrite a disputed entry yourself. It also affects isolation decisions at the unit: the attending checks the results and corrects it through the clinical workflow.
choices.then: You leave the entry and route the request to the attending.

vitals.log: Correction request logged; routed to author

choices.text: Tell her the chart cannot be changed.
choices.feedback: Correction is a right, not a favor. Route it to the author; if the author disagrees, that is documented and she is told why.

vitals.log: Correction request logged; routed to author

vitals.request: Census posted to wrong group chat

n4.scene: At 19:40 the charge nurse messages you: at 19:05 she posted the next day’s census, with names, patient numbers, and hepatitis status, to a barangay volunteer group chat instead of the staff group. About 40 people are in that chat.

choices.text: Report to the data protection officer now, within the hour; write down the facts (what, who, when sent, when discovered); keep a screenshot and do not delete anything until the DPO says how to contain it.
choices.feedback: You do not need to decide whether it is a breach; you need to report it. The 72-hour clock runs from the organization’s knowledge, so every hour lost at the front line is taken from the people who must decide.

choices.text: Report it on Monday morning; nothing can be done over the weekend.
choices.feedback: The clock does not stop for the weekend. Waiting until Monday leaves the controller only hours to decide.
choices.then: You reconsider and call the data protection officer at 20:15.

choices.text: Tell her to delete the post quickly and say nothing; it was only up for half an hour.
choices.feedback: Deleting quietly destroys the record of what was exposed and hides a possible breach from the people who must decide on notification. Sensitive health information was shared with about 40 people.
choices.then: You call the data protection officer at 20:00 and keep a record of the post.

n5.prompt: Who decides on notification, and when would it be due?

choices.text: The personal information controller, through its breach response team advised by the DPO; if required, notification to the National Privacy Commission and the affected patients is due within 72 hours of knowledge, about Monday 19:40.
choices.feedback: Under NPC Circular 16-03, notification is due within 72 hours of knowledge of a breach that requires it, based on the information available. The weekend counts. Your role is to report fast and record the facts; contacting patients or reassuring anyone is not yours.

choices.text: 72 working hours, so about Wednesday evening.
choices.feedback: The 72 hours are calendar hours from knowledge, not working hours. The weekend is part of the window.

choices.text: You decide; you will call the patients tonight and tell them it is probably fine.
choices.feedback: Do not contact affected patients yourself, and never reassure anyone that it is probably fine. The controller decides on notification and its wording.

end.title: Monday
end.text: The breach response team met on Saturday morning, had the post removed through the chat’s administrator with confirmation, and decided on notification before the deadline. The unit moves census sharing to its approved channel. Your release log shows every request of the day, including the three where nothing was released.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Five checks before any release: identity, authority, purpose, scope, channel.
  • Some requests are not yours to decide: police, media, lawyers, disputes. Log and route.
  • Correction is a right; the author corrects, the request stays on record.
  • Report a possible breach within the hour. The 72-hour clock runs from knowledge, weekends included.
  • Do not delete, investigate alone, or reassure.

See Five checks, Access and correction and The first hour.
